mainEntity.name: How much do dentures cost privately in London?

acceptedAnswer.text: The cost of private dentures in London varies depending on the type of denture, the materials used, and the complexity of your individual case. Partial dentures are generally less expensive than complete dentures. Premium materials such as chrome cobalt frameworks or highly customised tooth shades tend to increase the price. The most reliable way to obtain an accurate figure is to attend a dental consultation, where your dentist can assess your mouth and provide a personalised treatment plan with transparent pricing. Most reputable practices will give you a detailed written estimate before any work begins.

mainEntity.name: Can I get dentures on finance with bad credit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some dental finance providers may consider applications from patients with lower credit scores, although approval is not guaranteed. Each provider has its own eligibility criteria, and some practices may offer alternative payment arrangements for patients who are not approved for traditional finance. It is worth discussing your situation openly with your dental practice, as they may be able to suggest flexible payment options that work within your budget. Affordability assessments are carried out responsibly in line with financial regulations.

mainEntity.name: Are NHS dentures available in London?

acceptedAnswer.text: NHS denture treatment is available in some areas of London under Band 3, which has a fixed charge set by the NHS. However, availability can be limited, and waiting times may be longer than for private treatment. The range of materials and customisation options may also be more restricted. If you are eligible for NHS dental treatment, your dentist can discuss what is available and help you understand the differences between NHS and private denture options so you can make an informed decision.

mainEntity.name: How long do dentures last before they need replacing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dentures typically last between 5 and 10 years, although this depends on the quality of materials, how well they are maintained, and natural changes in your jawbone and gum tissue over time. Regular dental check-ups help monitor the fit and condition of your dentures. Relining — a process that adjusts the inner surface of the denture to improve fit — may be needed between replacements. If your dentures become loose, uncomfortable, or damaged, it is advisable to have them assessed rather than attempting repairs at home.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between partial and complete dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Partial dentures replace one or several missing teeth and are designed to fit around your remaining natural teeth. They are typically held in place by clasps or precision attachments. Complete dentures replace all the teeth in one or both arches and rely on suction, adhesion, or dental implants for retention. The choice between partial and complete dentures depends on how many teeth are missing, the health of remaining teeth, and your overall oral health. Your dentist can advise which option may be most appropriate following a clinical examination.

Denture adhesive can help improve the stability and comfort of well-fitting dentures, particularly for lower dentures where natural retention is more challenging. However, adhesive should not be relied upon to compensate for poorly fitting dentures. If you find yourself using increasing amounts of adhesive to keep your dentures in place, this may indicate that the fit has changed and a dental review is needed. Your dentist can assess whether relining, adjustment, or replacement is appropriate to restore a comfortable and secure fit.
